newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Cost controls help 1996 results - Cathay.
newsitem.headline: Cost controls help 1996 results - Cathay.

text.p: Stringent cost controls helped Cathay Pacific Airways Ltd boost profits, and the airline was confident it could continue to find ways to improve its cost structure, senior company executives said on Wednesday.
While total operating costs rose, boosted by higher fuel prices, unit costs fell.
"The point to highlight is that cost per ATK has fallen by five percent," said chairman Peter Sutch, refering to the company's 1996 earnings performance.
ATK stands for average tonne per kilometre and refers to capacity of both passenger and cargo shipping.
Cathay announced net profit of HK$3.81 billion in 1996, an increase of 27.9 percent over the previous year.
The bottom line was boosted by HK$541 million in exceptional gains from the sale of shares in Hong Kong Dragon Airlines Co Ltd to China National Aviation Corp.
Turnover grew by 6.33 percent on the back of a 12 percent rise in capacity, said managing director David Turnbull.
"This can be broken down into a 10 percent rise in passenger revenues and 14 percent rise in cargo revenue," Turnbull said.
Cathay Pacific Cargo reported turnover of HK$6.11 billion in 1996, up 5.6 percent over the year earlier, which accounted for 20.5 percent of the group's total traffic turnover.
"The number of passengers that we carried rose by 5.5 percent, while the number of cargo tonnes that we carried rose by 6.5 percent," said Turnbull.
"Unfortunately on the negative side, the yields that we attracted were down, down by 5.7 percent for passengers and 7.2 percent for cargo," he added.
Operating costs rose by HK$1.9 billion, or 7.14 percent.
"Significantly, the fuel price was very much higher, an increase of 21 percent but we were able after hedging to reduce that to a net 13 percent increase," said Turnbull.
The airline saved HK$281 million by hedging its fuel costs, and chairman Sutch said Cathay would continue refining that policy.
The airline also increased its cabin crew by 610 people, its ground staff in Hong Kong by 202, and its cockpit crew by 112, said Turnbull.
Still the airline was able to reduce unit costs.
"Unit cost per ATK did decline by five percent, despite the increase in fuel costs," repeated Turnbull.
As a result, operating profit was relatively stable, rising by HK$21 million to HK$3.79 billion.
"Financing costs were reduced, chiefly due to the cash inflow of HK$6.3 billion from the issue of 523 million new shares and also due to lower borrowing costs," added Turnbull.
Profit before exceptional items rose by 9.2 percent.
